Cubic Fields: A Primer

Sophie Marques and Kenneth Ward
Abstract.

We classify all cubic extensions of any field of arbitrary characteristic, up to isomorphism, via an explicit construction involving three fundamental types of cubic forms. We deduce a classification of any Galois cubic extension of a field. The splitting and ramification of places in a separable cubic extension of any global function field are completely determined, and precise Riemann-Hurwitz formulae are given. In doing so, we determine the decomposition of any cubic polynomial over a finite field.

MSC Code (primary): 11T22

MSC Codes (secondary): 11R32, 11R16, 11T55, 11R58

Keywords: Cyclotomy, cubic, function field, finite field, Galois

Introduction

In this paper, we give a complete classification of cubic field extensions up to isomorphism over an arbitrary field of any characteristic, which we had begun in [4]. More precisely, in Corollary 1.3, we prove that any cubic extension of an arbitrary field admits a generator yy, explicitly determined in terms of an arbitrary initial generating equation, such that

  1. (1)

    y3=ay^{3}=a, with a∈Fa\in F, or

  2. (2)
    1. (a)

      y3−3​y=ay^{3}-3y=a, with a∈Fa\in F, when p≠3p\neq 3, or

    2. (b)

      y3+a​y+a2=0y^{3}+ay+a^{2}=0, with a∈Fa\in F, when p=3p=3.

In §1.31.3, we devise a procedure to compare, up to isomorphism, any two separable cubic extensions of a given field. When the characteristic is not equal to 33, this employs the purely cubic closure which we determine in Theorem 1.4, whereas the Galois closure is needed in characteristic 3, eliminating the need for the brute force computations given in [4]. As we demonstrate, the purely cubic closure is essential for the study of cubic extensions which are not pure in characteristic distinct from 33. Furthermore, when the characteristic is equal to 3, the form (2)(a) we obtain can be viewed as a generalised Artin-Schreier form for separable extensions, where the techniques from Artin-Schreier theory can be adapted. We emphasize that all of our classifications (in any characteristic) are valid for any separable cubic extension.

For Galois cubics extensions L/FL/F, we prove in §1.4 that one of the following cases occurs, where each generator is again explicitly determined:

  1. (1)

    If p=3p=3, then L/FL/F is an Artin-Schreier extension; that is, there is a generator yy of L/FL/F such that y3−y=ay^{3}-y=a with a∈Fa\in F.

  2. (2)

    If p≠3p\neq 3 and FF contains a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, then L/FL/F is an Kummer extension; that is, there is a generator yy of L/FL/F such that y3=ay^{3}=a with a∈Fa\in F.

  3. (3)

    If p≠3p\neq 3 and FF does not contain a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, then L/FL/F is an extension with a generator yy of L/FL/F such that y3−3​y=2​a2+2​a−1a2+a+1y^{3}-3y=\frac{2a^{2}+2a-1}{a^{2}+a+1} with a∈Fa\in F.

Cases (1) and (2) are of course well known; we are able to deduce these again in a completely explicit and elementary way. Among Galois extensions, our primary focus is the third case, where Artin-Schreier and Kummer theory do not apply. We employ a generalised form of a Shank cubic polynomial in order to describe the Galois cubic extensions of the form (3) by way of an (explicit) one-to-one correspondence (Theorem 1.16). We also describe the Galois action on generators of the form (3) (Corollary 1.9); this is a consequence of Theorem 1.8, which determines when generators of the form (3) result in isomorphic extensions.

In §3, we describe the splitting and ramification for any place in a separable cubic extension of a global function field. To accomplish this, we use Kummer’s theorem to determine splitting of cubic polynomials over a finite field, as all residue fields are finite. Thus, in §2, we characterise completely the decomposition of any cubic polynomial over a finite field, using earlier results of Dickson, Pommerening, and Williams [2, 6, 12]. This study of decomposition permits us to obtain in §3.3 a Riemann-Hurwitz formula for any separable extension of a cubic global function field (Theorems 3.22, 3.24, 3.27).

While the classification we give for ramification, splitting, and genera is presented here for global function fields, many of the methods employed remain valid over any global field. As an example, we present Proposition 1.19, which characterises certain Galois cubic extensions and is proven separately over ℚ\mathbb{Q} and 𝔽q​(x)\mathbb{F}_{q}(x). We intend to produce a second study which addresses number fields, as there are substantive differences between the two types of global fields.

1. Classification of cubics over any field

In this section, we wish to obtain a complete and concise description of generating equations for cubic fields. The classification we obtain yields a family of three types of generating equations, all of which require only one parameter and are depressed, i.e., possess no quadratic term (§​1.1\lx@sectionsign 1.1). This classification is valid over any field. We note that of the families we obtain when p≠3p\neq 3 have generating equation X3−3​X−aX^{3}-3X-a; in this case, when −3-3 is not a square in FF, then the linear coefficient cannot be removed. We also provide a procedure permitting to determine whether any two cubic extensions are isomorphic (§1.3). When p≠3p\neq 3, in order to determine when two cubics are isomorphic, we make the use of the purely cubic closure (see Definition 1.1), which we determine precisely in §​1.2\lx@sectionsign 1.2. The purely cubic closure is important for studying impure cubic extensions (as we will see again in later sections, for instance, when we study ramification and splitting in §3). When p=3p=3, the Galois closure is used in the same way to find the analogous requisite criteria for isomorphism of two cubic extensions.

We then classify Galois cubics in any characteristic p≠3p\neq 3, which gives an analogue for all Galois cubic extensions which are not addressed in Artin-Schreier and Kummer theory. We show that the form we obtain in this case can be viewed as equivalent to a weaker form of a Shanks polynomial [8]. Curiously, we note that in the form

X3−3​X−2​a2+2​a−1a2+a2+1,X^{3}-3X-\frac{2a^{2}+2a-1}{a^{2}+a^{2}+1},

which we obtain when p≠3p\neq 3 and the extension is impurely cubic, the denominator a2+a+1a^{2}+a+1 of the constant coefficient is equal to an evaluation X2+X+1|X=aX^{2}+X+1|_{X=a} of the cyclotomic polynomial for primitive 3r​d3^{rd} roots of unity.

Henceforth, we let FF denote a field and p=char​(F)p=\text{char}(F) the characteristic of this field, where we admit the possibility p=0p=0 unless stated otherwise. We let F¯\overline{F} denote the algebraic closure of FF.

Definition 1.1.
  • ∙\bullet

    If p≠3p\neq 3, a generator yy of a cubic extension L/FL/F with minimal polynomial of the form X3−aX^{3}-a (a∈F)(a\in F) is called a purely cubic generator, and L/FL/F is called a purely cubic extension. If p=3p=3, such an extension is simply called purely inseparable.

  • ∙\bullet

    If p≠3p\neq 3 and a cubic extension L/FL/F does not possess a generator with minimal polynomial of this form, then L/FL/F is called impurely cubic.

  • ∙\bullet

    For any cubic extension L/FL/F, we define the purely cubic closure of L/FL/F to be the smallest extension F′F^{\prime} of FF such that L​F′/F′LF^{\prime}/F^{\prime} is purely cubic.

1.2. Purely cubic extensions

In order to obtain a complete classification of cubic extensions (up to isomorphism), we still need a criterion deciding when two cubic extensions are isomorphic. When p≠3p\neq 3, we have two possible types of generating equations: y3−3​y−ay^{3}-3y-a and y3−ay^{3}-a. So we first need to determine when the minimal equation y3−3​y−a=0y^{3}-3y-a=0 represents a purely cubic extension. In this section, we obtain a criterion for the coefficients of the minimal polynomial of a cubic extension L/FL/F which determines whether or not the extension is purely cubic.

Theorem 1.4.

Suppose p≠3p\neq 3. Let L/FL/F be a cubic extension and yy a primitive element with minimal polynomial

T⁡(X)=X3−3​X−aT(X)=X^{3}-3X-a

where a∈Fa\in F. Then, L/FL/F is purely cubic if, and only if, the polynomial S⁡(X)=X2+a​X+1S(X)=X^{2}+aX+1 has a root in FF. Let cc be a root of S⁡(X)S(X) in F¯\overline{F}. In other words, F⁡(c)F(c) is the purely cubic closure for L/FL/F. More precisely,

u=c​y−1y−cu=\frac{cy-1}{y-c}

is a purely cubic generator for L⁡(c)/F⁡(c)L(c)/F(c) such that u3=cu^{3}=c if, and only if,

y=c​u−1u−cy=\frac{cu-1}{u-c}

is a generator of L/FL/F with minimal polynomial T⁡(X)T(X).

Proof.

Suppose that p≠3p\neq 3. Let L/FL/F be a cubic extension and yy a primitive element such that y3−3​y−a=0y^{3}-3y-a=0. Any primitive element of L/FL/F is of the form u=e​y+fg​y+hu=\frac{ey+f}{gy+h} for e,f,g,h∈Fe,f,g,h\in F, since the elements of the set {y,u​y,u,1}\{y,uy,u,1\} are linearly dependent over FF. Moreover, e,ge,g are not both equal to 00, since uu is a primitive element. We wish to determine which extensions admit a primitive element uu such that u3=cu^{3}=c, for some c∈Fc\in F. Note that cc cannot be a cube, since L/FL/F is a cubic extension. We have that u3=cu^{3}=c and u=e​y+fg​y+hu=\frac{ey+f}{gy+h} is equivalent to

(−e3+c​g3)​y3+(−3​f​e2+3​c​g2​h)​y2+(−3​f2​e+3​c​g​h2)​y+c​h3−f3=0.(-e^{3}+cg^{3})y^{3}+(-3fe^{2}+3cg^{2}h)y^{2}+(-3f^{2}e+3cgh^{2})y+ch^{3}-f^{3}=0.

Corollary 1.12.

Let p=3p=3, and let y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} be two distinct roots in F¯\overline{F} of an irreducible polynomial X3+a​X+a2X^{3}+aX+a^{2}. Then y1=y2+l​by_{1}=y_{2}+lb, where b2=−ab^{2}=-a and l=1,2l=1,2.

1.4. Galois cubics

We conclude this section with the classification of Galois cubics. In this section, we will prove that if L/FL/F is a Galois cubic extension, then

  1. (1)

    If p=3p=3, then L/FL/F is an Artin-Schreier extension; that is, there is a generator yy of L/FL/F such that y3−y−ay^{3}-y-a with a∈Fa\in F.

  2. (2)

    If p≠3p\neq 3 and FF contains a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, then L/FL/F is an Kummer extension; that is, there is a generator yy of L/FL/F such that y3−ay^{3}-a with a∈Fa\in F.

  3. (3)

    If p≠3p\neq 3 and FF does not contain a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, then L/FL/F is an extension with a generator yy of L/FL/F such that y3−3​y−2​a2+2​a−1a2+a+1y^{3}-3y-\frac{2a^{2}+2a-1}{a^{2}+a+1} with a∈Fa\in F.

Parts (1)(1) and (2)(2) are well known; we include a proof to illustrate how these forms can be deduced directly from Corollary 1.3 to give a explicit Artin-Schreier (resp., Kummer) generator.

Theorem 1.13.

Let p=3p=3, let L/FL/F be a Galois extension of degree 33. Then there is a primitive element zz such that its minimal polynomial is of the form R⁡(z)=z3−z−aR(z)=z^{3}-z-a. Furthermore, this primitive element is explicitly determined.

Proof.

By Corollary 1.3, we know that there is a primitive element y′y^{\prime} such that its minimal polynomial is of the form

S⁡(X)=X3+b​X+b2.S(X)=X^{3}+bX+b^{2}.

The discriminant of such a polynomial is equal to −4​b3-4b^{3}. As L/FL/F is Galois, the discriminant is a square, thus −b-b is a square, say −b=a2-b=a^{2}. With y=y′/ay=y^{\prime}/a, it follows that y3−y=ay^{3}-y=a. ∎

In the case that p≠3p\neq 3, a cubic extension L/KL/K being Galois, FF containing a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity and L/KL/K being purely cubic are closely related as explained in the following theorem.

Theorem 1.14.

Let p≠3p\neq 3. Let L/FL/F be a cubic extension.

  1. (1)

    If FF contains a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, then L/FL/F is Galois if, and only if, it is purely cubic.

  2. (2)

    If L/FL/F is purely cubic, then L/FL/F is Galois if, and only if, FF contains a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity.

Proof.

Let p≠3p\neq 3. Let L/FL/F be a cubic extension.

  1. (1)

    Suppose that FF contains a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity ξ\xi.

    Suppose that L/FL/F is purely cubic. Then we may find a primitive element yy such that its minimal polynomial is y3=ay^{3}=a, for some a∈Fa\in F. In the usual way, the three elements yy, ξ​y\xi y, and ξ2​y\xi^{2}y are the roots of the minimal polynomial of yy, and they are all contained in LL. Thus, L/FL/F is Galois, and Gal​(L/F)=ℤ/3​ℤ\text{\emph{Gal}}(L/F)=\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}.

    Suppose now that L/FL/F is Galois, and let yy be a primitive element of L/FL/F with minimal equation y3+e​y2+f​y+g=0y^{3}+ey^{2}+fy+g=0. By Corollary 1.3, if 3​e​g=f23eg=f^{2}, then L/FL/F is purely cubic. Suppose then that 3​e​g≠f23eg\neq f^{2}. By Corollary 1.3, there exists a primitive element zz (which is explicitly determined) with minimal polynomial T⁡(X)=X3−3​X−aT(X)=X^{3}-3X-a. By Corollary 1.5, we have that L/KL/K is purely cubic, and Theorem 1.5 gives an explicit purely cubic genererator.

  2. (2)

    Suppose L/FL/F be a purely cubic extension, so that y3=ay^{3}=a for some a∈Fa\in F. As in [1, Theorem 2.3], L/KL/K is Galois if, and only if,

    1. ∙\bullet

      p≠2p\neq 2 and the discriminant Δ=−27​a2\Delta=-27a^{2} is a square in FF, which in turn is equivalent to FF containing a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, or

    2. ∙\bullet

      p=2p=2 and the resolvent polynomial R⁡(X)=X2+a​X+a2R(X)=X^{2}+aX+a^{2} is reducible, which is true if, and only if, X2+X+1X^{2}+X+1 is reducible, i.e., FF contains a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity.

∎

Theorem 1.14 proves that when FF contains a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, a cubic extension L/FL/F is Galois if, and only if, the extension L/FL/F is purely cubic. Particularly, when FF does not contain a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity and L/FL/F is Galois, then by Corollary 1.3, L/FL/F admits a primitive element with minimal polynomial of the form X3−3​X−aX^{3}-3X-a, where a∈Fa\in F. It follows that when p≠3p\neq 3, it remains to identify the Galois extensions with a generator with minimal polynomial of the form X3−3​X−aX^{3}-3X-a, where a∈Fa\in F.

Shanks studied Galois cubic extensions of ℚ\mathbb{Q} with generation

y3+a​y2−(a+3)​y+1,y^{3}+ay^{2}-(a+3)y+1,

where a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z} [8]. This led also to the definition of a Shanks cubic function field [7] as a Galois cubic extension L/𝔽q​(x)L/\mathbb{F}_{q}(x) with generating equation y3+a​y2−(a+3)​y+1y^{3}+ay^{2}-(a+3)y+1, where a∈𝔽q​[x]a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]. We note that over ℚ\mathbb{Q} or 𝔽q​(x)\mathbb{F}_{q}(x), the Shanks cubics so defined do not include all Galois cubic extensions. One may, however, show that any Galois cubic extension L/FL/F such that FF does not contain a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity admits a generator yy with minimal equation X3+a​X2−(a+3)​X+1X^{3}+aX^{2}-(a+3)X+1, where a∈Fa\in F. We give the proof of this, which A. Brumer shared with us in a helpful discussion; we will use this form to identify the missing Galois extensions.

Lemma 1.15.

Let p≠3p\neq 3. Suppose that FF does not contain a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity. A Galois cubic extension L/FL/F has a primitive element yy with minimal polynomial X3+a​X2−(a+3)​X+1X^{3}+aX^{2}-(a+3)X+1, where a∈Fa\in F. Let L=F⁡(z)L=F(z), and let Σ\Sigma be a generator of the Galois group Gal​(F​(z)/F)\text{\emph{Gal}}(F(z)/F). Then σ⁡(z)=Σ⁡(z)\sigma(z)=\Sigma(z), where

and

Theorem 1.16.

Let p≠3p\neq 3. Suppose that FF does not contain a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity. Let L/FL/F be a Galois cubic extension. Then there is a generator ww of L/FL/F whose minimal polynomial equal to

X3−3​X−2​b2+2​b−1b2+b+1,X^{3}-3X-\frac{2b^{2}+2b-1}{b^{2}+b+1},

Proof.

By Lemma 1.15, we have that there is a generator yy with minimal polynomial X3+a​X2−(a+3)​X+1X^{3}+aX^{2}-(a+3)X+1, where a∈Fa\in F. Via the change of basis

=(−(a2+3​a+9)−a⁡(a+6)a2−9a2+3​a+9)​w\displaystyle=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-(a^{2}+3a+9)&-a(a+6)\\ a^{2}-9&a^{2}+3a+9\end{array}\right)w
=−(a2+3​a+9)​w−a⁡(a−6)(a2−9)​w+a2+3​a+9=−(b2+b+1)​w−b⁡(b−2)(b2−1)​w+(b2+b+1).\displaystyle=\frac{-(a^{2}+3a+9)w-a(a-6)}{(a^{2}-9)w+a^{2}+3a+9}=\frac{-(b^{2}+b+1)w-b(b-2)}{(b^{2}-1)w+(b^{2}+b+1)}.

Remark 1.17.

We note that the quantity a2+a+1=(a+ξ)​(a+ξ2)a^{2}+a+1=(a+\xi)(a+\xi^{2}) in Theorem 1.16 is a norm of F⁡(ξ)F(\xi) over FF.

Suppose that F=KF=K is a global field, i.e., a function field over a finite field, or a number field. If the base field F=KF=K is a function field with field of constants 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, let 𝒪K,x\mathcal{O}_{K,x} denote the ring of integers of KK over 𝔽q​[x]\mathbb{F}_{q}[x], where x∈K\𝔽qx\in K\backslash\mathbb{F}_{q}. Then one can write the element bb in the Theorem 1.16 as b=ABb=\frac{A}{B} with A,B∈𝒪K,xA,B\in\mathcal{O}_{K,x}. If the base field KK is a number field, then the same can be done in OKO_{K}, the ring of integers over ℤ\mathbb{Z} in KK. We obtain the following corollary in terms of this decomposition.

Corollary 1.18.

Let KK be a global field which does not contain a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity, and let L/KL/K be a Galois cubic extension. Then there is a generator ww of L/KL/K with minimal polynomial equal to

X3−3​X−2​A2+2​A​B−B2A2+A​B+B2,X^{3}-3X-\frac{2A^{2}+2AB-B^{2}}{A^{2}+AB+B^{2}},

where A,BA,B lie in 𝒪K,x\mathcal{O}_{K,x} if K/𝔽qK/\mathbb{F}_{q} is a function field and 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} if KK is a number field.

Proposition 1.19.

Let K=ℚK=\mathbb{Q}, or K=𝔽q​(x)K=\mathbb{F}_{q}(x) with q≡−1mod3q\equiv-1\mod 3, and let L/KL/K a Galois cubic extension. By Theorem 1.16, L/KL/K has a primitive element with minimal polynomial of the form

with b=PQb=\frac{P}{Q}, where P,Q∈ℤ​o​r​𝔽q​[x]P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}\ or\ \mathbb{F}_{q}[x] such that (P,Q)=1(P,Q)=1. Then we have

Q=w​∏iQiei(ei∈ℕ)Q=w\prod_{i}Q_{i}^{e_{i}}\hskip 23.49976pt(e_{i}\in\mathbb{N})
  1. (1)

    if K=ℚK=\mathbb{Q}, then each QiQ_{i} is a prime number such that Qi≡1mod3Q_{i}\equiv 1\mod 3 and w=±1w=\pm 1; and

  2. (2)

    if K=𝔽q​(x)K=\mathbb{F}_{q}(x) with q≡−1mod3q\equiv-1\mod 3, then each Qi∈𝔽q​[x]Q_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x] is unitary and irreducible of even degree and w∈𝔽q∗w\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}.

Proof.

    By [5, Corollary 10.4], a prime number pp splits in ℚ⁡(ξ)\mathbb{Q}(\xi) if, and only if, p≡1mod3p\equiv 1\mod 3. Moreover, by [5, Proposition 10.2] , the ring of integers of ℚ⁡(ξ)\mathbb{Q}(\xi) is equal to ℤ⁡[ξ]\mathbb{Z}[\xi], and by [11, Theorem 11.1], the ring ℤ⁡[ξ]\mathbb{Z}[\xi] is a unique factorisation domain.     Qi=(Ai+ξ​Bi)​(Ai+ξ2​Bi)=Ai2+Ai​Bi+Bi2Q_{i}=(A_{i}+\xi B_{i})(A_{i}+\xi^{2}B_{i})=A_{i}^{2}+A_{i}B_{i}+B_{i}^{2}

    where Ai,Bi∈ℤA_{i},B_{i}\in\mathbb{Z} are coprime.

    By [3, Theorem 3.46], an irreducible polynomial over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} of degree nn factors over 𝔽qk​[x]\mathbb{F}_{q^{k}}[x] into gcd⁡(k,n)\gcd(k,n) irreducible polynomials of degree n/gcd⁡(k,n)n/\gcd(k,n).     with Ai,Bi∈𝔽q​[x]A_{i},B_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x] coprime.

Since in both cases, the norm map sending α+ξ​β\alpha+\xi\beta to α2+α​β+β2\alpha^{2}+\alpha\beta+\beta^{2} is multiplicative and K⁡(ξ)K(\xi) is a unique factorisation domain, we obtain the result. ∎

2. Decomposition of cubic polynomials over a finite field

Let 𝔽s\mathbb{F}_{s} denote a finite field with s=pms=p^{m} elements, where pp is a prime integer. In this section, we use the forms of Corollary 1.3 to obtain a simple characterisation of the irreducibility and splitting of cubic polynomials over any finite field. This will be needed for our detailed study of ramification and splitting for cubic function fields.

As it will be useful in a few results which follow, particularly in characteristics 22 and 33, we state the usual definition of the trace map from the finite field 𝔽s=𝔽pm\mathbb{F}_{s}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{m}} to the prime field 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}:

3. Ramification, splitting and Riemann-Hurwitz

In this section, we let F=KF=K denote a function field with field of constants 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, where q=pnq=p^{n} and p>0p>0 is a prime integer. We denote by 𝔭\mathfrak{p} a place of KK. The degree dK​(𝔭)d_{K}(\mathfrak{p}) of 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is defined as the degree of its residue field, which we denote by k⁡(𝔭)k(\mathfrak{p}), over the constant field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. The cardinality of the residue field k⁡(𝔭)k(\mathfrak{p}) may be written as |k⁡(𝔭)|=qdK​(𝔭)|k(\mathfrak{p})|=q^{d_{K}(\mathfrak{p})}. In an extension L/KL/K and a place 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of LL over 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, we let f(𝔓|𝔭)=[k(𝔓):k(𝔭)]f(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=[k(\mathfrak{P}):k(\mathfrak{p})] denote the inertia degree of 𝔓|𝔭\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}. We let e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}) be the ramification index of 𝔓|𝔭\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}, i.e., the unique positive integer such that v𝔓​(z)=e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)​v𝔭​(z)v_{\mathfrak{P}}(z)=e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})v_{\mathfrak{p}}(z), for all z∈Kz\in K. If v𝔭​(a)≥0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)\geq 0, then we let

a¯:=amod𝔭\overline{a}:=a\mod\mathfrak{p}

denote the image of aa in k⁡(𝔭)k(\mathfrak{p}).

Here, we study the ramification and splitting of places in cubic function fields over KK, and we give an explicit Riemann-Hurwitz formula for separable cubic function fields over KK. We obtain these results for any prime characteristic pp, using the classification given in Corollary 1.3, which establishes that any separable cubic extensions L/KL/K has a generator with minimal polynomial equal to one of the following:

  1. (1)

    X3−aX^{3}-a, a∈Ka\in K, when p≠3p\neq 3

  2. (2)

    X3−3​X−aX^{3}-3X-a, a∈Ka\in K, when p≠3p\neq 3

  3. (3)

    X3+a​X+a2X^{3}+aX+a^{2}, a∈Ka\in K, when p=3p=3.

We would like to point out that by Corollary 1.3, if p≠3p\neq 3, then every impure cubic extension L/KL/K has a primitive element yy with minimal polynomial of the form

f⁡(X)=X3−3​X−a.f(X)=X^{3}-3X-a.

We mention this here, as we will use it whenever this case occurs in §3. When this is used, the element yy will denote any such choice of primitive element.

3.1. Constant extensions

In this subsection, we wish to determine when a cubic function field over KK is a constant extension of KK. We do this before a study of ramification and splitting, as constant extensions are unramified and their splitting behaviour is well understood [10, Chapter 6]. In the subsequent subsections, we will thus assume that our cubic extension L/KL/K is not constant, which, as 3 is prime, is equivalent to assuming that the extension is geometric.

Let p≠3p\neq 3, and let L/KL/K be purely cubic, i.e. there exists a primitive element y∈Ly\in L such that y3=ay^{3}=a, a∈Ka\in K. 3.2. Splitting and ramification

In this section, we describe the splitting and ramifcation of any place of KK in a cubic extension L/KL/K. As usual, we divide the analysis into the three fundamental cubic forms derived in Corollary 1.3.

Remark 3.4.

Given any place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK, one may always choose (via weak approximation) an element x∈K\𝔽qx\in K\backslash\mathbb{F}_{q} such that 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is not above the pole divisor 𝔭∞\mathfrak{p}_{\infty} of xx in 𝔽q​(x)\mathbb{F}_{q}(x). for a nonempty, proper subset SS of the collection of all places of LL. (2) 𝔭𝒪L,x=𝔓1e⁡(𝔓1|𝔭)⋯𝔓re⁡(𝔓r|𝔭),\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_{L,x}=\mathfrak{P}_{1}^{e(\mathfrak{P}_{1}|\mathfrak{p})}\cdots\mathfrak{P}_{r}^{e(\mathfrak{P}_{r}|\mathfrak{p})},

When a purely cubic extension L/KL/K is separable, one may also easily determine the fully ramified places in L/KL/K.

Theorem 3.6.

Let p≠3p\neq 3, and let L/KL/K be a purely cubic extension. Given a purely cubic generator yy with minimal polynomial X3−aX^{3}-a, a place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK is fully ramified if, and only if, (v𝔭​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1.

3​v𝔓​(y)=v𝔓​(y3)=v𝔓​(a)=e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)​v𝔭​(a).3v_{\mathfrak{P}}(y)=v_{\mathfrak{P}}(y^{3})=v_{\mathfrak{P}}(a)=e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a).

Since (v𝔭​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1, we obtain 3|e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)3|e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}), and as e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)≤3e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})\leq 3, it follows that e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=3e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=3, so that 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is fully ramified in LL.

    irreducible modulo 𝔭\mathfrak{p},

Theorem 3.9.

Let p≠3p\neq 3, and let L/KL/K be an impurely cubic extension and yy primitive element with minimal polynomial f⁡(X)=X3−3​X−af(X)=X^{3}-3X-a. Then the fully ramified places of KK in LL are precisely those 𝔭\mathfrak{p} such that v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0 and (v𝔭​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1.

Proof.

As usual, we let ξ\xi be a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity. We also let rr be a root of the quadratic resolvent R⁡(X)=X2+3​a​X+(−27+9​a2)R(X)=X^{2}+3aX+(-27+9a^{2}) of the cubic polynomial X3−3​X−aX^{3}-3X-a in K¯\bar{K}. As in [1, Theorem 2.3], we know that L⁡(r)/K⁡(r)L(r)/K(r) is Galois, and by Corollary 1.5, we have that L⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r)/K(\xi,r) is purely cubic. We denote by 𝔭\mathfrak{p} a place in KK, 𝔓ξ,r\mathfrak{P}_{\xi,r} a place of L⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r) above 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, 𝔓=𝔓ξ,r∩L\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}_{\xi,r}\cap L, and 𝔭ξ,r=𝔓ξ,r∩K⁡(ξ,r)\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}=\mathfrak{P}_{\xi,r}\cap K(\xi,r). By Corollary 1.5, we know that that L⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r)/K(\xi,r) is Kummer; more precisely, there exists v∈K⁡(ξ,r)v\in K(\xi,r) such that v3=cv^{3}=c where cc is a root of the polynomial X2+a​X+1X^{2}+aX+1.

We thus obtain a tower L⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ)/KL(\xi,r)/K(\xi,r)/K(\xi)/K with L⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r)/K(\xi,r) Kummer of degree 33, and where K⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ)K(\xi,r)/K(\xi) and K⁡(ξ)/KK(\xi)/K are both Kummer extensions of degree 22. As the index of ramification is multiplicative in towers and the degree of L⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r)/K(\xi,r) and K⁡(ξ,r)/KK(\xi,r)/K are coprime, the places of KK that fully ramify in LL are those places of KK which lie below those of K⁡(ξ,r)K(\xi,r) which fully ramify in L⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r)/K(\xi,r). As L⁡(ξ,r)/K⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r)/K(\xi,r) is Kummer, the places of K⁡(ξ,r)K(\xi,r) that ramify in L⁡(ξ,r)L(\xi,r) are described precisely by Kummer theory (see for example [10, Example 5.8.9] as those 𝔭ξ,r\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r} in K⁡(ξ,r)K(\xi,r) such that

(v𝔭ξ,r​(c±),3)=1.(v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}}(c_{\pm}),3)=1.

Lemma 3.8 states that if v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0, then v𝔭ξ,r​(c±)=±v𝔭ξ,r​(a)v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}}(c_{\pm})=\pm v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}}(a) and that otherwise, v𝔭ξ,r​(c±)=0v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}}(c_{\pm})=0. Thus, the ramified places of L/FL/F are those places 𝔭\mathfrak{p} below a place 𝔭ξ,r\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r} of K⁡(ξ,r)K(\xi,r) such that (v𝔭ξ,r​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}}(a),3)=1. Also,

v𝔭ξ,r​(a)=e⁡(𝔭ξ,r|𝔭)​v𝔭​(a),v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}}(a)=e(\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}|\mathfrak{p})v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),

where e⁡(𝔭ξ,r|𝔭)e(\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}|\mathfrak{p}) is the ramification index of a place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK in K⁡(ξ,r)K(\xi,r), equal to 11, 22, or 44, and in any case, coprime with 33. Thus, (v𝔭ξ,r​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi,r}}(a),3)=1 if, and only if, (v𝔭​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1. As a consequence of the above argument, it therefore follows that a place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK is fully ramified in LL if, and only if, v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0. ∎

This theorem yields the following corollaries, the first being immediate.

Corollary 3.10.

Suppose that q≡−1mod3q\equiv-1\mod 3. Let L/KL/K be a Galois cubic extension, so that there exists a primitive element yy of LL with minimal polynomial f⁡(X)=X3−3​X−af(X)=X^{3}-3X-a. Then the (fully) ramified places of KK in LL are precisely those places 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK such that v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0 and (v𝔭​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1.

Corollary 3.11.

Suppose that q≡−1mod3q\equiv-1\mod 3. Let L/KL/K be a Galois cubic extension, so that there exists a primitive element yy of LL with minimal polynomial f⁡(X)=X3−3​X−af(X)=X^{3}-3X-a. Proof.

In Lemma 3.8, it was noted that σ⁡(c±)=c∓\sigma(c_{\pm})=c_{\mp} where Gal​(K⁡(c±)/K)={I​d,σ}\text{\emph{Gal}}(K(c_{\pm})/K)=\{Id,\sigma\}, when c±∉Kc_{\pm}\notin K. Let ξ\xi again be a primitive 3r​d3^{rd} root of unity. We denote by 𝔭\mathfrak{p} a place of KK and 𝔭ξ\mathfrak{p}_{\xi} a place of K⁡(ξ)K(\xi) above 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. We find that

v𝔭ξ​(c±)=vσ⁡(𝔭ξ)​(σ⁡(c±))=vσ⁡(𝔭ξ)​(c∓).v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\pm})=v_{\sigma(\mathfrak{p}_{\xi})}(\sigma(c_{\pm}))=v_{\sigma(\mathfrak{p}_{\xi})}(c_{\mp}).

Note that if σ⁡(𝔭ξ)=𝔭ξ\sigma(\mathfrak{p}_{\xi})=\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}, it follows that v𝔭ξ​(c±)=v𝔭ξ​(c∓)v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\pm})=v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\mp}). However, by Lemma 3.8, we have that, for any place 𝔭ξ\mathfrak{p}_{\xi} of K⁡(ξ)K(\xi) above a place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK such that v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0, it holds that v𝔭ξ​(c±)=±v𝔭ξ​(a)v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\pm})=\pm v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(a), and that v𝔭ξ​(c±)=−v𝔭ξ​(c∓)v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\pm})=-v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\mp}). Thus, for any place 𝔭ξ\mathfrak{p}_{\xi} of K⁡(ξ)K(\xi) above a place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK such that v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0, we find that v𝔭ξ​(c±)≠v𝔭ξ​(c∓)v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\pm})\neq v_{\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}}(c_{\mp}) and thus σ⁡(𝔭ξ)≠𝔭ξ\sigma(\mathfrak{p}_{\xi})\neq\mathfrak{p}_{\xi}. Therefore, by [10, Theorem 6.2.1], we obtain that 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is of even degree, for any place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK such that v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0. ∎

Corollary 3.12.

Suppose that q≡−1mod3q\equiv-1\mod 3. Let L/KL/K be a Galois cubic extension, so that there exists a primitive element yy of LL with minimal polynomial f⁡(X)=X3−3​X−af(X)=X^{3}-3X-a. Then one can choose a single place 𝔓∞\mathfrak{P}_{\infty} at infinity in KK such that v𝔓∞​(a)≥0v_{\mathfrak{P}_{\infty}}(a)\geq 0.

Proof.

One can choose x∈K\𝔽qx\in K\backslash\mathbb{F}_{q} such that the place 𝔭∞\mathfrak{p}_{\infty} at infinity for xx has the property that all of the places in KK above it are of odd degree. In order to accomplish this, we appeal to a method similar to the proof of [10, Proposition 7.2.6]; because there exists a divisor of degree 1 [10, Theorem 6.3.8], there exists a prime divisor 𝔓∞\mathfrak{P}_{\infty} of KK of odd degree; for if all prime divisors of KK were of even degree, then the image of the degree function of KK would lie in 2​ℤ2\mathbb{Z}, which contradicts [10, Theorem 6.3.8]. Let dd be this degree. Let m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} be such that m>2​gK−1m>2g_{K}-1. Then, by the Riemann-Roch theorem [10, Corollary 3.5.8], it follows that there exists x∈Kx\in K such that the pole divisor of xx in KK is equal to 𝔓∞m\mathfrak{P}_{\infty}^{m}. By definition, the pole divisor of xx in k⁡(x)k(x) is equal to 𝔭∞\mathfrak{p}_{\infty}. It follows that

(𝔭∞)K=𝔓∞m,(\mathfrak{p}_{\infty})_{K}=\mathfrak{P}_{\infty}^{m},

from which it follows that 𝔓∞\mathfrak{P}_{\infty} is the unique place of KK above 𝔭∞\mathfrak{p}_{\infty}, and by supposition that 𝔓∞\mathfrak{P}_{\infty} is of odd degree. From this argument, we obtain that, with this choice of infinity, all places above infinity in k⁡(x)k(x) are of odd degree. (We also note that we may very well choose mm relatively prime to pp, whence K/k⁡(x)K/k(x) is also separable; in general, K/k⁡(x)K/k(x) as chosen will not be Galois.)

As q≡−1mod3q\equiv-1\mod 3, L/KL/K is a Galois extension, and yy is a primitive element with minimal polynomial of the form X3−3​X−aX^{3}-3X-a where a∈Ka\in K, we know that all of the places 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK such that v𝔭​(a)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0, and in particular, all the ramified places, are of even degree (see Corollary 3.11). It follows that the process described in this proof gives the desired construction, and the result follows. ∎

Remark 3.13.

We note that when KK is a rational function field, one may use Corollary 3.12 to show that the parameter aa has nonnegative valuation at 𝔭∞\mathfrak{p}_{\infty} for a choice of xx such that K=𝔽q​(x)K=\mathbb{F}_{q}(x), and thus such 𝔭∞\mathfrak{p}_{\infty} is unramified.

We now turn to a determination of splitting in impurely cubic extensions. We remind the reader that in what follows, as in Remark 3.4, while the integral closure 𝒪L,x\mathcal{O}_{L,x} of 𝔽q​[x]\mathbb{F}_{q}[x] in LL depends upon the choice of xx, the residue field k⁡(𝔭)k(\mathfrak{p}) of a place 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of KK does not.

3.3. Riemann-Hurwitz formulae

Using the extension data, it is possible to give the Riemann-Hurwitz theorem for each of our forms in Corollary 1.3. These depend only on information from a single parameter.

3.3.1. X3−aX^{3}-a, a∈Ka\in K, p≠3p\neq 3

Lemma 3.21.

Let p≠3p\neq 3. Let L/KL/K be a purely cubic extension and yy a primitive element of LL with minimal polynomial f⁡(X)=X3−af(X)=X^{3}-a. Let 𝔭\mathfrak{p} be a place of KK and 𝔓\mathfrak{P} a place of LL over 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. Then the following are true:

  1. (1)

    d⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=0d(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=0 if, and only if, e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=1e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=1.

  2. (2)

    d⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=2d(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=2, otherwise. That is, by Theorem 3.7, e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=3e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=3, which by Theorem 3.6 is equivalent to (v𝔭​(a),3)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.7, either e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=1e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=1 or e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=2e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=2.

  1. (1)

    As the constant field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} of KK is perfect, all residue field extensions in L/KL/K are automatically separable. The result then follows from [10, Theorem 5.6.3].

  2. (2)

    If e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=3e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=3, then as p∤3p\nmid 3, it follows again from [Theorem 5.6.3, Ibid.] that d⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=e⁡(𝔓|𝔭)−1=2d(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=e(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})-1=2.

∎

We thus find the Riemann-Hurwitz formula as follows for purely cubic extensions when the characteristic is not equal to 3, which resembles that of Kummer extensions, but no assumption is made that the extension is Galois.

Theorem 3.22 (Riemann-Hurwitz I).

Let p≠3p\neq 3. Let L/KL/K be a purely cubic geometric extension, and yy a primitive element of LL with minimal polynomial f⁡(X)=X3−af(X)=X^{3}-a. Then the genus gLg_{L} of LL is given according to the formula

gL=3​gK−2+∑(v𝔭​(a),3)=1dK​(𝔭).g_{L}=3g_{K}-2+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1\end{subarray}}d_{K}(\mathfrak{p}).
Proof.

This follows from Lemma 3.23, [10, Theorem 9.4.2], and the fundamental identity ∑eifi=[L:K]=3\sum e_{i}f_{i}=[L:K]=3. ∎

We are now able to state and prove the Riemann-Hurwitz formula for this cubic form.

Theorem 3.24 (Riemann-Hurwitz II).

Let p≠3p\neq 3. Let L/KL/K be a cubic geometric extension and yy a primitive element of LL with minimal polynomial f⁡(X)=X3−3​X−af(X)=X^{3}-3X-a.     where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of places of KK such that both a≡±2mod𝔭a\equiv\pm 2\mod\mathfrak{p} and v𝔭​(Δ,2)=1v_{\mathfrak{p}}(\Delta,2)=1. Moreover, the set 𝒮\mathcal{S} is empty when Δ\Delta is a square in KK.

    gL=3​gK−2+12​∑𝔭∈𝒮[−v𝔭​(1a2+1−w𝔭2+w𝔭)+1]​dK​(𝔭)+∑v𝔭​(a)<0(v𝔭​(a),3)=1dK​(𝔭),g_{L}=3g_{K}-2+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathfrak{p}\in\mathcal{S}}[-v_{\mathfrak{p}}\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+1-w_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}+w_{\mathfrak{p}}\right)+1]d_{K}(\mathfrak{p})+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a)<0\\ (v_{\mathfrak{p}}(a),3)=1\end{subarray}}d_{K}(\mathfrak{p}),

    where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of places of KK such that both a≡0mod𝔭a\equiv 0\mod\mathfrak{p} and there exists w𝔭∈Kw_{\mathfrak{p}}\in K such that v𝔭​(1a2+1−w𝔭2+w𝔭)<0v_{\mathfrak{p}}\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+1-w_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}+w_{\mathfrak{p}}\right)<0 and (v𝔭​(1a2+1−w𝔭2+w𝔭),2)=1(v_{\mathfrak{p}}\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+1-w_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}+w_{\mathfrak{p}}\right),2)=1. Moreover, the set 𝒮\mathcal{S} is empty when r∈Kr\in K.

Proof.
  1. (1)

    By [10, Theorem 9.4.2], the term associated with a place 𝔓\mathfrak{P} of LL in the different 𝔇L/F\mathfrak{D}_{L/F} contributes 12​dL​(𝔓)d⁡(𝔓|𝔭)\frac{1}{2}d_{L}(\mathfrak{P})^{d(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})} to the genus of LL, where 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is the place of KK below 𝔓\mathfrak{P}, dL​(𝔓)d_{L}(\mathfrak{P}) is the degree of the place 𝔓\mathfrak{P}, and d⁡(𝔓|𝔭)d(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}) is the differential exponent of 𝔓|𝔭\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}. By the fundamental identity ∑ieifi=[L:K]=3\sum_{i}e_{i}f_{i}=[L:K]=3 for ramification indices eie_{i} and inertia degrees fif_{i} of all places of LL above 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, we always have that fi=1f_{i}=1 whenever 𝔭\mathfrak{p} ramifies in LL (fully or partially). Thus from Lemma 3.23, it follows that d⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=2d(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=2 if 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is fully ramified, whereas d⁡(𝔓|𝔭)=1d(\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p})=1 if 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is partially ramified.
